title: Complex Convergence
body:
A complex [[Sequence]] $z_n$ converges to $L$ when $|z_n - L| \to 0$, where $|\cdot|$ is the modulus.
That is the same $\varepsilon$ definition as [[CALCULUS 2]] with absolute value read as distance in
the plane, and it splits cleanly: **$z_n \to L$ if and only if $\operatorname{Re}z_n \to
\operatorname{Re}L$ and $\operatorname{Im}z_n \to \operatorname{Im}L$**. Two real convergence
questions, no new machinery.

Series work the same way. $\sum z_n$ converges when its partial sums do, and absolute convergence
($\sum|z_n| < \infty$) still implies convergence, so **every test in [[Convergence Tests]] that
only looks at magnitudes carries over unchanged**: ratio, root, comparison. The ones that need
order, like the alternating series test, do not, because $\mathbb{C}$ is not ordered.

## Power series and the radius of convergence

$\sum a_n(z - z_0)^n$ converges inside a **disc** rather than an interval. There is a radius $R$,
computed by the same ratio or root limit as in [[Power Series]], such that the series converges
absolutely for $|z - z_0| < R$ and diverges for $|z - z_0| > R$, with the boundary circle needing
its own examination.

The disc is where complex analysis explains something real analysis could only observe. The
Maclaurin series of $\frac{1}{1+x^2}$ has radius 1 on the real line, and nothing about the real
function suggests why: it is smooth everywhere, with no bad behaviour at $x = \pm 1$. Over
$\mathbb{C}$ the answer is immediate. **The function blows up at $z = \pm i$**, which sit at distance
1 from the origin, and the disc of convergence can never reach a singularity. See [[Taylor Series]]
and [[Maclaurin Series]] in [[CALCULUS 2]]; this is the note that answers the question they leave
open.

That is also the general shape of the subject: a complex-differentiable (analytic) function is
automatically infinitely differentiable and equal to its own Taylor series on any disc avoiding its
singularities, which is nothing like the real case. [[Complex Integration]] and the
[[Residue Theorem]] are what you do with the singularities once you know where they are.

The iteration in [[Mandelbrot Set]] is a convergence question of exactly this kind, asked pointwise:
does the orbit stay bounded or run off to infinity?
